spec.title: PROP-066 — Remap: replaceable artifact sources for closed networks, shared as packages

status.comment: Drafted 2026-10-31 on the owner's request. R-1 built 2026-11-01: the row model, the consent-free layers, the Locator, adoption by every fetch path, and `remap list` / `explain`. R-2 built 2026-11-01: remap packages, consent and its flags, the provider map, uninstall behaviour, `remap test`, `export` / `import`, `cache import`, the `[requires.remaps]` pin, and the lock provenance sidecar. `fetched_from` lives in `vibe.lock.provenance` rather than on the lock row, because the lock refuses unknown fields — this paragraph's own fallback (`#provenance`).

p.purpose: A vibe installation must work where the public hosts are unreachable, filtered, or forbidden by policy: no internet, a corporate network that allows one artifact store, a security team that names the only places bytes may come from. Every artifact vibe fetches gets a replaceable source, the replacement is declared once as data, and the declaration travels between people as an ordinary package. The failure this avoids is the one the owner met in NixOS: everything nailed to one public host, with no layer in between to point elsewhere.

p.principle: Identity is content, location is a replaceable detail. Everything vibe downloads already carries a hash (`vibe.lock` `content_hash`, `sha256` of application inputs, the publisher's digest in `DISTRIBUTIONS.json`, `content_hash` of embedded sources). A remap changes only where bytes are looked for; the bytes are verified against the same hash as before, so a remap can make a fetch fail or succeed but never change what is installed. Different bytes need a new capture and review, never a fallback that accepts them (`campaigns/next` R-027).

p.row: A remap is one `[[remap]]` row with three parts. **What** it matches, exactly one of: `sha256 = "<hex>"` (any artifact declared with that digest, whatever its URL); `package = "<group>/<name>[@<req>]"` (the registry package, its index entries and its embedded sources); `registry = "<name>"` (every URL a declared registry resolves to, including its index and raw-file endpoints); `prefix = "<url prefix>"` (every URL starting with it, the host rewrite). **With** what, exactly one of: `url = "…"` (an `https://`, `http://`, `file://` or git URL; for `prefix` the matched prefix is replaced by it, for the other keys it is the whole new location), `path = "…"` (a local file or directory; a directory is searched as `<path>/<sha256>/<filename>` the way the application download cache is laid out), or `deny = true` (the fetch is refused before any connection with the error code `remap_denied`, naming the row and its reason). **Where** it applies, optional: `scope = { package = "…" }` or `scope = { package = "…", step = "ID" }` limits a row to the installation of one application package or one of its steps. Every row may carry `reason`, shown by `explain` and in refusals.

p.row-offer-description: A package carrying rows may describe the whole offer in `[remap] description = "…"` (what network this is for, who maintains it, where to ask), and that text heads every question and listing about it. The description is a property of a remap package, so it arrives with `#package` and `#consent`.

p.diagnostics: Being sent to another address is suspicious by nature, so every place a remap is shown says what a reader needs to judge it, computed, never trusted from the package: the target host and scheme (`https`, plain `http` marked `unencrypted`, `file://` and `path` marked `local`, git over ssh marked by its host), whether the host is a private address or a public one, how many of the package's rows point at each host, which rows are `deny`, and which rows widen scope (a `prefix` row over a public host is marked `broad`). A row whose target cannot be classified is shown as `unknown`, not hidden. `explain` adds, for one fetch, the full chain: declared origin, every matching row in winning order with its package, layer and reason, the chosen target, and the digest that will be checked.

p.diagnostics-reachability: Every view also states whether the target answered a `HEAD` the last time `remap test` ran, and when. The record is `<home>/remap/reachability.json`, written by `remap test` itself (`#policy`), which is what performs the probe; a target with no record says nothing rather than guessing, and a view never re-probes to fill the line.

p.precedence: When several rows match one fetch the most specific key wins: `sha256`, then `package`, then `registry`, then `prefix` (the longest prefix among prefixes). A scoped row beats an unscoped row of the same key. Among equally specific rows the one from the higher layer of `#layers` wins, and inside one layer the later row. `vibe remap explain <url|sha256>` prints every matching row in winning order with its set and layer, so a surprising choice is one command away.

p.layers: Rows come from four layers, lowest first: remap packages the user has accepted in the user home (`#consent`); remap packages the project requires in `vibe.toml` (`#layers-packages`); local rows in `.vibe/settings.local.toml` and `~/.vibe/settings.toml` (`[[remap]]` tables, for one developer's machine, no acceptance needed because the user wrote them); and the invocation, `--remap <file.toml>` (repeatable) or `VIBE_REMAP=<file>[,<file>]`. The existing registry `[[mirror]]` and `[[override]]` tables of PROP-002 stay as they are and are read as rows of the local layer (`registry = …` and `package = …` respectively), so nothing a user wrote stops working. The two package layers are ranked here and produced by nothing until `#consent` lands; the hardcoded single-file endpoints of PROP-002's HTTPS fast path are the default rows beneath all four.

p.layers-packages: A project requires remap packages in `vibe.toml` as `[requires.remaps]`, resolved and locked like any dependency so every clone of the project sees the same offer, applied on each machine only after that user's acceptance (`#consent`). The pin is `vibe.lock`'s own `[[remap]]` table — key, version, content hash, registry — and not a `[[package]]` row: a remap package is never materialised into `vibedeps/` and no package may depend on one (`#decisions`), so it has a table of its own rather than a kind inside the dependency closure. The acceptance is bound to the pinned content hash, so a clone that resolves a different version is asked again rather than inheriting a yes.

p.package: Any vibepack may carry `[[remap]]` rows and an optional `[policy]` table; a package whose manifest declares `[package] kind = "remap"` carries nothing else and nothing executable. Either way the rows are an **offer**, never an obligation: installing the package records the offer and applies no row until the user accepts it (`#consent`). A remap package is versioned, content-hashed, published to any registry (an internal one included), installed with `vibe install -g` into the user home or required by a project, listed by `vibe list -g`, and removable like any package. Several accepted packages are read in their acceptance order unless a package declares `priority = N` (higher wins among packages). This is how a colleague's or an architect's list reaches a team: publish it, require it, or hand it over on a disk; each person then decides whether their machine follows it. A `remap`-kind manifest carries only `[package]`, `[compatibility]`, the `remap` key and `[policy]`, and must carry at least one row; every other table is a validation error naming the table, because accepting a redirection must never be a way to run someone's code. TOML cannot carry `[remap]` and `[[remap]]` in one document — they are a redefinition error — so the key is read in either of two shapes: the bare array of rows, or a table carrying `description`, `priority` and its rows under `[[remap.rows]]`. A package with no description writes the array; one that describes its offer writes the table.

p.consent: Acceptance is per user home and bound to the package's content hash: `vibe remap accept <package>` records it, `vibe remap reject <package>` records the refusal so the question is not asked again, and a new version of an accepted package is a new offer. **The default is always a question.** When a run would apply an offer that is neither accepted nor rejected, an attended terminal shows the package, its reason, every row it carries (what each one redirects and to where, and what it denies) and asks `apply the N remap rows?` with `no` as the default — the question is a PROP-067 `#question` block: `? remap offer` in the gutter, the offered package and its rows as its body, the prompt as its last line, and the answer collapsing to `✓ remap offer accepted <package>` or `rejected <package>` while the body stays above it as the record of what was answered; an unattended run (`--json`, no terminal, `--yes` absent) refuses with `consent_required`, naming `vibe remap accept <package>`. The flags: `--accept-remap` (install, update and every verb that resolves artifacts) accepts every offer the run meets, `--accept-remap <package>` (repeatable) accepts named ones, `--reject-remap` rejects every unasked offer for this run without recording anything; `vibe install -g <remap package> --accept-remap` installs and accepts in one go. An offer that is rejected or still unanswered is listed by `vibe remap list` as `offered` or `rejected`, and `vibe remap enable|disable` switches an accepted package off and on without removing it or forgetting the acceptance. A graphical client gets the same question through the `consent_required` envelope and answers it with `accept`. A run that applies no row asks nothing: the read-only `remap` verbs are where the question is being answered, and installing or removing a remap package records or retires an offer rather than applying one — a home with one pending offer must still be able to install a second remap package. Likewise a verb that only reads local state — `vibe app launchers`, `vibe app work`, `vibe cache check` and their kin, the verbs a desktop shell polls — asks nothing and refuses nothing; among `vibe app` and `vibe cache` only `plan`, `modify`, `outdated`, `rollback` and `cache add` resolve artifacts and so may ask.

p.providers: The home keeps a map of its active rows: for every row the packages that offer it (`<home>/remap/providers.json`, derived from the installed packages and the acceptance ledger `<home>/remap/consent.json`, rebuilt whenever either changes, never the sole home of a fact). Two rows are the same when key, target and scope are equal. `vibe remap list` shows each row with its providers, so a row many accepted packages share reads differently from one a single package brought. The map is what uninstall consults.

p.uninstall: Uninstalling a package that offers accepted rows never silently changes what the machine fetches from. Before removing, vibe shows the rows that would stop applying (those with no other accepted provider), the rows that stay because another package still offers them, and asks `keep these N rows as local rows? [Y/n]`: `yes` copies the orphaned rows into the user home's local layer with `from = "<package>@<version>"` and the original reason, so the machine keeps working and `list` still says where each row came from; `no` drops them. The flags `--keep-remap` and `--drop-remap` answer without asking; unattended runs without a flag refuse with `consent_required` the same way acceptance does. The acceptance record itself is deleted with the package.

p.display: Every human view of remaps is one layout, aligned the way `PROP-065#plan` aligns a plan: a header block (the source file or package the rows came from, its layer, the policy it declared), one numbered block per row (`N. <key kind> <what>` on the first line, then indented `to <target> [<scheme>, <private|public|local>]`, `why <reason>`, `scope …` and `from …` when present, and a `note` line for `unencrypted`, `broad` or `unknown`), and a footer summarising targets per host (`3 rows → nexus.corp.example (https, private); 1 row → local path; 1 deny`). `list`, `explain` and their `--json` documents carry the same fields in the same order, so a graphical client renders the same blocks. Nothing is abbreviated to fit: long targets wrap under their label, and `--json` is the escape for machines. The look — the rule per source, the dim labels, the accent keys, the warn notes — is PROP-067's (`#heading`, `#palette`, `#inline`).

p.display-packages: A package's own header block carries its key and version, its `description`, the registry it came from and its state; the consent question and the uninstall question use the same layout and the same field order as `list` and `explain`.

p.policy: `[policy] unmatched = "allow" | "deny"` in a remap package or a local layer: with `deny`, any fetch no row matches is refused before a connection with the error code `remap_denied`, naming the URL, the hash and the sets consulted. The strictest policy of all active layers applies. `vibe remap test` walks a project's or a home's declared artifacts (lock entries, application inputs of installed packages, the distribution manifest) and reports which row each one resolves to and whether the target answers a `HEAD`, without downloading, so a policy can be checked before it bites.

p.locator: One resolution point in `vibe-core` (`Locator`) is the only way a crate turns a declared source into the places to try. Its input is the artifact's identity (kind, declared URL or git locator, digest when declared, the package and step it belongs to); its output is the ordered candidate list with the winning row attached, or a `deny` refusal. Every fetch path adopts it: registry clones, redirects and git-source dependencies (PROP-002), the index and raw-file endpoints (PROP-005; the hardcoded `raw.githubusercontent.com` and `gitverse.ru` table becomes the default rows, which apply to single-file reads only — a registry clone, a git-source dependency, an embedded source, an application input or an index file of the same host keeps its declared origin, because the endpoint serves one file at a time and a `git clone` of it is a 404), embedded sources (PROP-021; the cache key becomes the content hash so the same bytes from another host hit), application inputs of `sources`, `archive` and `native` steps (PROP-059, PROP-065; `archive` and `native` inputs gain the same `<sha256>` cross-run cache `sources` have), `vibe self` distributions (PROP-019: the release base and the `DISTRIBUTIONS.json` location become remappable and the check that refused a non-GitHub base is dropped; the source-install mirror list accepts a remapped clone URL), the documentation shell (PROP-057), and the install scripts (`VIBEVM_RELEASE_ORIGIN` honoured, not only declared). The one `[proxy]` table (`https`, `http`, `no_proxy`) in settings reaches reqwest and child `git` through the same point.

p.locations: One rule decides which locations bytes may be read from, shared by `vibe self bootstrap`, `self update`, `self install` and `install -g` (`ByteLocation` in `vibe-core`): `https://` and `http://` URLs are remote — the controlled transport and the source policy decide whether they may be contacted; a `file://` URL and a `path` target are local and are read directly, never handed to HTTP, with any query (the release lane's cache-buster) dropped; a relative path or any other scheme is refused before any I/O with a fix naming the accepted spellings. A `prefix` row with a `path` target treats the directory as a mirror of the URL layout: the URL remainder after the prefix is joined onto the directory segment by segment, query and fragment dropped and no segment climbing out (`..`); for an application input the directory itself is still searched by digest as before.

p.drops: An **artifact drop** is a directory a person fills by hand plus a naming convention, declared in `~/.vibe/config.toml` `[artifacts]`: `vibe = "<dir>"` (vibe releases, read by `vibe self` through PROP-019 `#release-sources`) and `packages = "<dir>"` (application payloads). A drop is not a second routing mechanism and adds no artifact kind: `packages` lowers into one `local`-layer row (source `[artifacts] packages`) for `app-input` artifacts only, the weakest row a user can have, ranked above only the declared origin, so every user, project or invocation row still wins and `vibe remap list` / `explain` show it. An input declared `url + sha256` by package `G/N@V` is looked for under the drop at `G/N/V/F`, then `G/N/F`, then `D/F` (the digest), then `F`, where `F` is the last path segment of the declared URL; a rung that would climb out of the drop is skipped. **The digest is always verified**: a wrong file is a `digest_mismatch` refusal and is not kept, never silently used. A miss names the exact expected file name, the digest and every path searched, and the next candidate (the declared origin) is still tried; when the source policy excludes the origin's host the drop's miss is reported first. `vibe artifacts where [<package>] [--registry DIR] [--json]` prints the release drop layout for the running version and target, the package drop convention, and with a package every downloaded input of every installer option with its file name, digest, searched paths and state (`present`, `mismatch`, `missing`, `no-drop`); `--json` is `vibe-artifacts-where/1`. A relative drop path is ignored with a warning naming the fix — but a drop path that starts at the reader's own home is NOT relative: `vibe = "~/opt/drop/releases"` and `packages = "~/opt/drop/packages"` (and `~\<rest>` on Windows) are resolved against the same home directory `~/.vibe` comes from, by the one rule of PROP-019 `#install-root` `##INSTALL-ROOT-HOME`, so one site profile names each developer's own drops and the file keeps the `~` it was written with; `~user` is refused by the key that carries it.

p.drops-author: A package built inside a closed network may declare a `sources` input that has no URL at all: `drop = "packages"`, `file = "<name>"` and `sha256` (exactly one of `url`, `path` or `drop`; `packages` is the one drop; `file` is one portable file name and appears only with `drop`). The input is resolved through the same convention as `#drops`, in every configured `[artifacts] packages` drop, highest layer first, verified against its digest and cached by digest like any downloaded input; no configured drop is a refusal naming `[artifacts] packages`. `vibe app describe --json` and the installer-option documents carry `drop` and `file` (optional fields of `source_input` in `application_describe`, `application_installer_options` and `configuration/e1/description`). An `archive` or `native` step's `source` stays a URL or a package-relative path; a closed-network package declares such a payload as a `sources` input.

p.not-covered: What a recipe script does on its own (`curl`, `git clone`, `pip install` inside a `recipe` step) is outside vibe's fetches and outside this PROP. Such a step declares `needs = "network"` (PROP-065), and under a `deny` policy the plan marks it `needs network, not remappable` — a `note` on the plan's step row, beside the `needs` line and distinct from the `skipped:` reason, so the reader sees it before the build starts. The recommended package shape in a closed network is to declare such downloads as `[[sources]]` inputs with digests, which this PROP then covers.

p.provenance: Where bytes came from is recorded beside what they are. `fetched_from` (the URL actually used) was to sit next to the canonical `source_url` on every `vibe.lock` `[[package]]` row on the understanding that an older vibe ignores a field it does not know; it does not — every lockfile struct carries `deny_unknown_fields`, so the extra key would make an older binary unable to read the lock at all, and this paragraph's own fallback applies: the fact is recorded in the sidecar `vibe.lock.provenance` beside the lock, which an older vibe never opens, regenerated on every install and resolved from by nothing. Further: application run records and `steps.json` record per input the candidate that served it and the row that chose it; the install record of `vibe self` names the base used. `--json` reports carry the same fields. Nothing in a manifest or a lock is rewritten to the remapped URL, so a lock stays portable between networks and the canonical origin stays visible for review.

p.transport: Getting the first set into a closed network: `vibe remap export <package> --out <dir> [--with-artifacts]` writes a `file://` registry holding the remap package and, with `--with-artifacts`, every artifact its rows and the current project's lock name, laid out by digest; `vibe remap import <dir>` (or plain `vibe install -g --registry <dir> <package>`) installs from it, and `vibe cache import <dir>` places the artifacts into the machine store and the application download cache by their digests, verifying each. The existing `vibe registry vendor` stays the way to vendor registry packages; `export --with-artifacts` calls it.

p.commands: `vibe remap list [--json]` (rows by source and layer, with the policy each declared and the strictest one in force) and `explain <url|sha256> [--json]`. Both are read-only, both emit `vibe-remap/1` documents under `--json`, and a fetch refused before any connection carries the code `remap_denied` (`#row`). The remaining verbs are `#commands-packages`; a verb vibe cannot honour does not appear in its help.

p.commands-packages: `vibe remap test [--json]`; `accept|reject <package>`; `enable|disable <package>`; `export`; `import`. With `list` and `explain` these complete the `vibe-remap/1` surface, which is the only interface a graphical client needs: a remap package shows as an installed package with its state and a switch (`offered` / `accepted` / `rejected` / `disabled`), an unanswered offer shows as a question with its rows, `explain` answers a hover, `test` fills a readiness panel, and the provenance fields of a run record show which row served each download of an installation.

p.acceptance: Public Linux fixtures, in two files. The consent-free half (`cli_remap.rs`): an application `sources` input served by a `sha256` row from a directory with the test server counting zero hits, a `prefix` row rewriting one server's URL to a second, the same input refused by a `deny` row with the row and its reason named, `unmatched = "deny"` refusing an unlisted URL before any connection, `--remap` beating a settings row, and the two read-only views including the per-host footer. The consent half (`cli_remap_packages.rs`): a remap package installed from a `file://` registry into a scratch home shows as `offered` and applies nothing (the input still comes from the origin); an unattended install of an application then refuses with `consent_required` naming `vibe remap accept <package>` before any fetch; `--accept-remap` on that install applies the row with the server never asked; a rejected package is not asked about again; `disable` and `enable` switch an acceptance without forgetting it; two packages offering one row show both providers and the derived map is on disk; uninstalling one of them keeps the row, uninstalling the last refuses unattended and `--keep-remap` copies the orphan into the user's own `[[remap]]` table with `from` and the original reason while `--drop-remap` lets it go; `remap test` reports a row pointing at a closed port as unreachable and exits 1, and every view then states that answer with its date; a `remap`-kind package carrying `[[binary]]` is a validation error naming the table; `export --with-artifacts` then `import` into a second scratch home is followed by an `--offline` install that asks no server; an `archive` input is cached across runs by its digest, so a second install after `app work --clean` makes no server hit. Unit fixtures cover the ledger, the provider map, the kept-row round trip and the offer's row provenance. **Left to the manual lane**: the lock provenance sidecar end to end (it needs a git registry pair with a live mirror, not a `file://` directory) and MT-07 on a host with networking cut — install an application and update vibe through a remap package served from a directory.

p.decisions: Decision: remaps are data rows keyed by digest, package, registry or prefix, carried by an installable package, resolved at one point, verified by the unchanged digests. Why: digests already exist for everything fetched; a package is the one unit vibe already versions, hashes, publishes, installs and lists, so sharing and the graphical client come for free. A remap is an offer a user accepts, because a package author must not be able to redirect another person's downloads by being installed. Rejected: environment variables per host (they cannot be shared or reviewed and they leak); rewriting URLs inside manifests or locks (loses provenance, breaks portability between networks); a fallback that accepts a mirror's different bytes (the Nix lesson, and R-027); a remap package that other packages may depend on (policy belongs to the user and the project, never to a dependency). Open for the owner: whether `[proxy]` belongs in a remap package as well as in settings, and whether a project may forbid user-home packages from applying (`[remap] project_only = true`).

p.supersedes: PROP-002 `TRUST-MIRROR-HATCH` (`--trust-mirror`, specified and never shipped) is withdrawn: no flag accepts a mirror's different bytes. PROP-002 `vibe list --overrides` (specified, never shipped) is replaced by `vibe remap list`, which shows the `[[override]]` and `[[mirror]]` rows as the local layer. PROP-002's tables themselves stay; this PROP adds keys to them and a resolution point above them.

p.client: For a graphical client the whole surface is: `remap list --json` for the catalog of packages and rows with their states and diagnostics; the `consent_required` envelope as the question, answered with `remap accept` or `remap reject`; `remap explain --json` for a hover on any download of a plan or a run record; `remap test --json` for a readiness panel; `uninstall` of a providing package answered with `--keep-remap` or `--drop-remap` after the client shows the orphaned rows. The client never reads or writes `consent.json`, `providers.json` or any TOML of the layers.

p.changelog: 2026-11-03 — `#locator`: the built-in single-file rows apply to single-file reads only; since 1.0.9 they also rewrote git-source dependencies and other one-URL clones of github.com and gitverse.ru to the single-file endpoint, and the clone failed. 2026-10-31 — drafted; renamed from substitutions to remap; consent, diagnostics, providers, uninstall, display and client surface added; PROP-002 tails marked. 2026-11-01 — R-1 built: `#row`, `#precedence`, `#locator`, `#diagnostics`, the consent-free `#layers`, and `#commands` / `#display` for `list` and `explain` are `spec/done`; the error code `remap_denied` named; the package, consent, provider, uninstall, transport and `remap test` halves split into their own paragraphs and left `spec/work`. 2026-11-01 — R-2 built: remap packages and the `remap` package kind (VIBEVM-SPEC §4.1 amendment), the acceptance ledger and its flags, the derived provider map, the uninstall question and its kept local rows, `remap test` with the reachability record, `export` / `import` / `cache import`, the `[requires.remaps]` pin in `vibe.lock`, the `fetched_from` sidecar, and the `<sha256>` cross-run cache for `archive` and `native` inputs. Every paragraph is `spec/done` and the document is closed. 2026-11-01 — `#consent`: the question is a PROP-067 `#question` block.
